hits.name: wast3
hits.text:
Anthropic put a model on a bacterium dragged out of a place nothing should survive, and it turns out the thing feeds on an element that kills almost everything else.

What it eats is only half of it. The other half is that it does the job faster than the organisms we engineer for the same task.

> ISOLATE - the strain separated from the site, no lab-friendly conditions added
> FEED - every input it accepts tested one at a time, including the toxic ones
> TRACE - each element followed through the cell to see what it becomes
> SWAP - the pathway compared against the version every other microbe uses
> LOAD - the strain pushed until output stops, to find where the limit sits
> MATCH - the result measured against the engineered strains built for this job

Toxicity is usually a wall. An element that wrecks a normal cell stops the process before anything useful comes out.

This one built a route around the damage. The same element goes in, and the pathway simply refuses to break.

Nobody designed that. It evolved somewhere the alternative was not surviving at all.

The engineered strains we use for this cost years of work and still run slower than something that was already there.

That gap matters more than the discovery itself. Nature solved it under pressure nobody would choose to reproduce in a lab.

Most environments like this one are written off before sampling, because nothing is expected to be alive in them.

Every input it accepts, the pathway map and the throughput numbers sit in the breakdown below.

→ ignore gets dropped with a 1% audit, forever
→ log gets written to the ledger with no ping
→ draft goes to Grok Bot, then into a review queue
→ human is you, with all 3 answers attached
→ Ledger Bot sends the bill every morning at 09:00

3. Append every decision to ledger.jsonl with the answers, lane, audit flag and token estimate. Sample 1% of ignored events into queue/audit

4. Write → that prints jev cost, writing cost, jev share and escalation rate, and flags escalation above 6%
